topic: Compiler-Synthesized Move Operations for Classes with Built-in Types
explanation: In C++, when a class consists of movable members (such as built-in types like int or std::string), the compiler can automatically generate move constructors and move assignment operators if they are not explicitly defined. This is a practical technique for improving performance in real-world scenarios, such as when working with containers, returning large objects from functions, or managing resources efficiently. Best practices include relying on compiler-synthesized moves to keep code idiomatic and concise, but always check for potential issues like non-movable members (e.g., const objects or references). Common pitfalls include assuming moves will always be synthesized— if a class has user-defined copy operations or non-movable members, the compiler won't generate them, leading to unnecessary copies or compilation errors. In practice, this pattern enhances efficiency in applications like game development or data processing, where object movement reduces overhead.
